📌 Bridges and Cross-Chain Swaps: Where Hacks Happen

Main Points
⏺ Cross-chain services hold large pools of user funds in shared vaults
⏺ When their keys or code fail, liquidity providers take the loss
⏺ This post explains the risk and how to limit your exposure



1️⃣ Core Idea — A bridge or cross-chain swap does not move your coins between chains. It locks them in a vault on one side and pays you out on the other. Whoever controls that vault controls the money.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Vaults are run by signing keys, validators or smart contracts. If any of them is compromised, an attacker can drain everything at once.
3️⃣ Example — Over the weekend Chainflip lost about $12 million, including 122.86 BTC, after a suspected compromise of its signing key. Its services were paused.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Liquidity you deposit in bridge pools, swaps left pending mid-route, unlimited token approvals, and fake "recovery" sites that appear after every hack.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Use bridges only to move funds, not to store them. Swap, confirm arrival, revoke approvals, and keep only what you can afford to lose in cross-chain pools.
Final Thoughts

Bridges are useful, but they concentrate risk. Treat every cross-chain step as a short trip, not a place to park your crypto.

📈 BlackRock Drives $541M Single-Day Bitcoin ETF Outflow

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $582 million in net outflows on Thursday, November 19 — their third consecutive day of redemptions — as Bitcoin slipped below $62,000.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541 million of that figure, marking its largest single-day outflow on record. For the week, Bitcoin ETFs shed a combined $1.12 billion, with BlackRock responsible for $899 million of the total. Ether ETFs added $131 million in outflows on the same day, pushing combined BTC and ETH redemptions above $713 million for Thursday alone.

The week's outflow streak marks one of the sharpest stretches of institutional selling since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in January 2024.

Ukraine Faces a Grim Reality as U.S.-Mediated Peace Talks Resume


After more than eight months without direct negotiations, Russia and Ukraine resumed U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi last week. But the battlefield and political realities have changed significantly since February. Moscow’s demands remain largely unchanged, while its confidence in achieving them has grown.

The central issues remain Ukraine’s exclusion from NATO and Russia’s control over most or all of Donbas. The author argues that Russia has effectively won the war and that Ukraine is running out of time to negotiate before its position deteriorates further.

Ukraine is suffering devastating military and demographic losses. Thousands of soldiers are being killed or wounded, millions of citizens have fled, and many are unlikely to return. Declining birth rates, rising mortality and mass emigration are undermining the country’s workforce and economic future.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ability to defend itself is weakening. Western supplies of air defense interceptors are insufficient, while Russian missiles and drones continue striking critical infrastructure. Ports, industrial facilities, transportation networks and energy systems have all suffered extensive damage. Regular blackouts in Kyiv illustrate the growing strain on civilian life.

Russian forces are also making gradual advances across Donbas. The author argues that Kyiv should acknowledge the military reality and consider territorial concessions to prevent further casualties.

The article maintains that Russia’s invasion was never primarily about territory, but about preventing Ukraine from joining NATO and securing Moscow’s claimed interests in Donbas. The failure of the Minsk agreements and the subsequent military buildup contributed to the Kremlin’s decision to pursue territorial control.

Washington appears increasingly open to a negotiated settlement involving changes to Ukraine’s borders. Trump has suggested that Ukraine will emerge from the conflict with a different territorial configuration. Reports indicate that Kyiv may privately consider compromises, provided it receives credible security guarantees.

However, Ukraine continues to reject recognition of Russian control over its territory, either legally or in practice. Zelensky has also questioned proposals to exchange Donbas for security arrangements that would fall short of NATO membership.

The fundamental dilemma remains: Ukraine wants lasting security without surrendering territory, while Russia insists on conditions that Kyiv considers unacceptable. Until that gap is bridged, negotiations may struggle to produce peace.

📣 MEXC shuts down Visa-linked crypto card less than three months after launch 

🌐 Cryptocurrency exchange MEXC has announced that it will discontinue its Global Card payment services on Nov. 18 at 15:30 UTC, less than two weeks after U.S. authorities issued an order restricting its access to the American financial system. The exchange did not identify the issuing partner or specify whether its decision was directly related to the recent enforcement action by the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

📊 During the maintenance period, customers could transfer their remaining card balances to their exchange accounts, while transactions initiated before the suspension remained subject to normal settlement procedures. MEXC had initially described the interruption as temporary but has now confirmed that the service will not resume as scheduled.

🔗 Cardholders could receive cashback ranging from 4% to 10%, with monthly rewards capped at up to 800 USDT depending on their eligibility. Applications were already unavailable to U.S. residents under the exchange’s regional restrictions. Customers using the card for recurring payments have been advised to cancel their subscriptions or register alternative payment methods to avoid interruptions once the card becomes inactive.
